cards.title: Decide Between Founder Handle and Company Page for Partnership Ads
cards.summary: Choose where to run founder-led paid social based on which page has relevant content volume and whether you want brand or person association.
cards.use_when: Deciding which ad account/page identity to run founder creative from on Instagram/Meta for an ecommerce brand.
steps: Check content volume on both the founder's personal handle and the brand page: the source notes the page with more frequent, relevant posting tends to perform better because the ad inherits social proof from that profile's content.

Judge relevance, not lifestyle: the source stresses the personal page must have founder-store-relevant content, not just photos of the founder with a dog at the park — non-relevant content gives little lift.
If neither page has relevant content, the source says default to running through the company page: it builds brand association and avoids the risk that customers buy 'you' rather than the brand.

Weigh the efficiency trade-off: running as a partnership ad through the founder handle can give an efficiency boost, but it makes sales depend on the founder, which the source flags as a risk for brands that want to be bought for the company.
Treat this as a per-brand decision, not a fixed rule; the source explicitly says it is not one-or-the-other for everyone and that for many people keeping it on the same page is fine.
caveats: This is the presenter's situational recommendation, not a universal rule; there is no benchmark for how much lift a personal handle delivers.
Platform partnership-ad mechanics and eligibility change — verify current requirements in the ad platform interface.

cards.title: Three Elements of the Dishwashing-Sheet Founder Ad
cards.summary: A high-performing founder ad combined a negative hook, fast pacing, and showing the product working in the first three seconds.
cards.use_when: Writing or storyboarding a cold-audience founder ad for a consumable ecommerce product.
steps: Open with a negative or apologetic hook (the example: 'I need to publicly apologize to anyone who's ever bought these dishwashing sheets before, because I lied') combined with fast pacing so the opening does not read as an ad.
Show the product working within the first three seconds — the source says this hooks the viewer by proving efficacy immediately alongside the hook.
Put the founders front and center in the marketing so the brand reads as founder-led, which the source argues builds immediate trust because they put their reputation on the line.

Lean into an underdog narrative: in the example, two brothers from a small market taking on large incumbents associated with harsh chemicals — a positioning the source says almost any small business can adopt by telling its story.
Build the story and positioning into the creative itself rather than leaving it only on the brand's About page.
caveats: The source presents this as an example of a winning ad, not a measured causal test; treat as a pattern to test, not a guarantee.

Showing the product in the first seconds conflicts with other examples in the same source (see the natural-deodorant ad, where the presenter preferred holding the product back) — the right choice depends on awareness stage and format.

cards.title: Use Format Innovation to Stop the Scroll
cards.summary: Running an ad in a format the audience has never seen before stops the scroll because viewers wonder what the content is.
cards.use_when: Planning creative concepts for cold-audience ecommerce acquisition when standard founder-to-camera formats are fatiguing.
steps: Audition formats, not just scripts: the source's example is a story-based ad shot professionally where the speaker talks to a crowd in a store, and the shots are rarely on the speaker's face.
Use novelty to create a curiosity gap — the presenter reports being hooked specifically because he had never seen ad content in that format, which made him want to know what story was coming.

Pair the unfamiliar format with a genuine story: the source says whenever you can weave a story into ad creative it performs better, and that the most obvious version is a founder story but it does not have to be one (the example tells the origin of a specific product).

When structuring the edit, consider holding on the speaker longer: the presenter identified rapid cutting away to product shots and B-roll (some with out-of-sync audio) as the weakness, because each cut reminded him he was watching an ad.
Test an alternate cut that removes that B-roll or delays the product until at least roughly the 20-second mark.
caveats: The '20-second mark' suggestion is the presenter's personal preference, not a tested threshold.
The claim that story-based ads 'always' perform better is the source's opinion — no comparative data is given — so validate on your own account.

cards.title: Sequence an Ad as Hook, Curiosity Gap, Objection Handling, Benefits
cards.summary: A strong founder ad can be built in a deliberate sequence: credibility hook, curiosity gap, warehouse social proof, objection handling, then benefits over features.
cards.use_when: Scripting a founder product ad for an ecommerce brand, especially a supplement or food product with a common objection.
steps: Open with a credibility hook that signals legitimacy — the example opens with the product having taken over two years of development.
Immediately open a curiosity gap (the example: 'and here's why') to pull the viewer forward before explaining anything.
Insert social proof visually as the founder walks through the warehouse, so the audience sees scale/operations while listening.
Bridge into objection handling: the example names every negative attribute of competing products ('gluggy, gritty, grainy, and gluey') before making any claim about his own.
Move to benefits instead of features — smooth and creamy, under 1g of sugar, budget-friendly — after objections have been cleared.

Name the product only after the problem and benefits are established, and keep the CTA from opening new curiosity loops the ad then never closes (the source criticizes 'forget everything you know about pea protein' because it bridges nowhere).
caveats: The source flags the re-opened curiosity gap and the CTA as weaknesses in this otherwise strong ad — do not copy them.
No performance numbers are given; this is a structural commentary, not a tested result.

cards.title: Problem-Agitation Arc Ending in Scarcity
cards.summary: A contrarian hook followed by escalating problem agitation across alternative solutions, then a founder story and scarcity close, made a protein-jerky ad work end to end.
cards.use_when: Writing acquisition creative for a food or supplement brand entering a category with entrenched but flawed incumbents.
steps: Open with a contrarian claim about the category ('the protein industry is broken') paired with fast-paced graphics to hook attention.
Agitate the problem against the viewer's daily reality and their ideal self, naming the specific persona ('you want more muscle... but every protein snack you see is ultra-processed').

Extend agitation to competing solutions — the example dismisses beef jerky as soy, sugar and low-quality minced meat and not even high in protein, then notes typical jerky isn't made for lifters — so the viewer has no good alternative left.
Introduce the founder story here: he designed something from steak, salt and spice; he quit his job, posted daily for a year, grew to over 100,000 followers and shipped across his country.
Close with scarcity placed after the founder story ('I sell out all the time, but right now I've got stock'), then the CTA to get delivery to the door.
caveats: This is a case-study narrative of one ad the presenter rates highly; the follower count and shipping claims are the brand's, not benchmarks.
Agitation must be factually defensible — the source does not instruct making unsupported negative claims about competitors.

cards.title: Founder Story Scripting from Personal Problem Onward
cards.summary: A founder ad scripts the actual sequence of the founder's own problem, self-solutioning, material choices, and present-day proof.
cards.use_when: Structuring a long-form founder origin story for a product brand, even at large scale, and especially when AI-generated creative is flooding the feed.
steps: Start with the founder's own specific problem in first person and concrete physical detail (the Step One example: hiking, chafing, big legs, wearing bike shorts, sweating).
Move into self-solutioning as relatably scrappy as possible — the example cuts up one pair of bike shorts and sews panels just between the legs, then notices the result.

Walk through how materials and design decisions were reached (testing bamboo as a fabric, adding elastic around the pouch so it lifts, separates and supports) — the source calls this scripting 'really good' because each step follows the previous.
Note that the brand built connection and a human presence, which the source says is especially valuable now that AI creative is flooding ad accounts.
Close with risk reversal and social proof — in the example, a 30-day wear-and-if-you-don't-love-them-they're-free guarantee and 'join over 2 million customers' — plus a direct link CTA.
Know that production value is not the constraint: the source notes this ad was shot on an iPhone, likely scripted in 5–10 minutes, walking around a park.
caveats: The source's claim that a big $100M-scale brand running its first founder ad means founder ads are 'crushing for them' is the presenter's inference, not verified data.
The 30-day guarantee and 2 million customers are that brand's facts, not templates for other brands.

cards.title: Match Ads to the Stages of Awareness
cards.summary: Place most creative in early awareness stages and roughly 20% at product/solution-aware stages, because a bottom-funnel ad cannot educate a cold audience.
cards.use_when: Allocating creative concepts across prospecting and retargeting campaigns, or diagnosing why an ad with good engagement isn't scaling.
steps: Diagnose each ad by what the viewer must already know to understand it. The source's example: a hemp/rosehip oil ad opens with testimonials about how good the product is — that only works for people already product aware.
Recognize the failure mode: for unaware audiences the ad introduces the product immediately with no problem education and no top-of-funnel agitation, so it can't resonate.
Follow the source's stated allocation heuristic: put most ads in awareness stages one, two and three, with about 20% in stages four and five.
Assign the product-aware testimonial-style ad to bottom of funnel, where it can convert people who just need a few video testimonials to tip them over.
Before buying large cold reach behind any ad, confirm it contains enough educational or problem-framing material to make sense to someone who has never heard of you.
caveats: Treat the 20% split as the source's heuristic, not a calculated benchmark.
The source reports the oil ad had generated about half a million dollars in revenue to date — a single case example, not a promise for similar creative.

cards.title: Founder Story Built on a Discovered Ingredient
cards.summary: A colostrum-gummies founder ad stacked a shocking hook, a family-transformation story, objective proof, and a manufacturing credibility reveal.
cards.use_when: Building acquisition creative for a supplement or ingestible brand with a novel delivery format.
steps: Open with a hook and a matching visual that are genuinely unusual (here, the founder citing the quantity of breast milk/colostrum bought so she could make the first gummy of its kind), then promise the explanation ('you're wondering how I got here, let me explain').
Tell a concrete transformation story: the founder's mother had long-term gut issues, took colostrum, and reported gut lining repair plus hair and skin benefits.
Pair the subjective family claim with objective proof by pulling in scientific studies — the source notes this pairing as the reason the claim lands rather than reading as pure anecdote.
Name the real consumer friction that justifies the product ('powdered colostrum is hydrophobic, so you choke down a chalky mess') so the gummy format has a reason to exist.

Establish supply-chain credibility with specifics: eight months of work, a named farm producing high-grade first-day-milking whole colostrum, a gummy manufacturer that preserves integrity, and the first 5,000 bags produced.
End with a next-step CTA (follow to get first access) rather than an immediate hard sell.
caveats: Health-outcome claims made by founders require your own regulatory/compliance review; claims in the example are not validated by the source.
No performance metrics are given for this ad.

cards.title: Sequencing Proof Before Product Reveal
cards.summary: A premium toothbrush ad front-loads a founder story and problem agitation and delays the product reveal, letting low-fi founder footage contrast with premium product shots.
cards.use_when: Creating acquisition video for a premium-positioned product where you want to justify the price before showing the product.
steps: Open by building authority through the founder's credentials (time spent in dental labs) and then state a category-level claim the big brands 'hope you never notice'.

Build stakes with a concrete, quantified research story: they bought every top-rated electric toothbrush, spent thousands of dollars on name brands with celebrity ads and $300 price tags, and used them for months.

Agitate on the discovered problems — porous plastic absorbing bathroom moisture, charging bases acting like Petri dishes collecting black mould where the brush is stored, Bluetooth apps added to justify markup — before any product is shown.

Reveal the solution only after agitation, with specific materials and spec choices (aircraft-grade aluminum vice plastic, 14 motor frequencies tested to settle on 32,000 micro-vibrations per minute, wall mount instead of countertop stand, 60-day battery).

Use the contrast deliberately: the source notes low-fi founder footage early does not damage a premium brand as long as the product is not introduced in that lower-quality footage — it creates contrast with the later high-end product shots.
Close on the positioning line and a comparison CTA inviting the viewer to upgrade from a name brand that stopped caring.
caveats: The claim that low-fi footage is safe 'as long as the product isn't introduced at the same time' is the presenter's reasoning, not a tested result.
Volume of proof claims must be legally defensible; the source gives no guidance on substantiation.

cards.title: Diagnose Bottom-Funnel-Only Creative Portfolios
cards.summary: An ad library built entirely on a founder's personal brand and late-stage objections cannot scale on cold audiences.
cards.use_when: Auditing a brand's existing creative library before scaling spend or when evaluating a celebrity/founder-fronted ad account's structure.
steps: Audit the library for awareness-stage spread: the source's example brand runs ads that read as bottom-of-funnel because they open with testimonials, taste, and value framing only meaningful to someone already sold.
Check whether the ad assumes viewers know the spokesperson — the source says anyone who doesn't already know the figure will not watch that far, so reach is capped at the existing audience.

Look for objections that belong at the point of purchase being used as acquisition messages: 'it tastes great' and 'cheaper than buying all the pills separately' are, per the source, close-only objection handling, not cold-audience value propositions.
Ask the cold-audience questions the ad must answer: what is in the product, why should I care about any of those ingredients, who is this person, and why should I trust them.

If a few bottom-funnel ads run alongside strong top-of-funnel creative, that's fine — the problem is when the entire library sits there and the account can only capitalise on the founder's existing audience.
caveats: This is the presenter's diagnosis of an example library, without account data; do not treat it as proof about any specific brand's efficiency.
Some brands deliberately concentrate on an existing fanbase — the source treats that as a reason scaling will stall, not as inherently wrong.

It's very low on organic volume, but my page, my individual Instagram, has enormous amounts of content on it and there's content going up every 2 hours on that page. And so inherently, obviously, we would have better performance when we run as a partnership ad through the personal page over the company page. And so you just have to weigh these things up, okay? Are you a small business as a founder and you don't care about it running through your personal page and does your personal page have content on it? Really important. And I'm not saying like photos of you at the park with your dog, like I mean photos that are relevant to the founder store, okay? Whereas if it doesn't, then you're probably not going to get much lift doing this. You probably just want it running through the company page. And then you're going to build brand and association and affiliation with the company and you're not posing this risk point where people are buying you instead. So that's where this becomes a a very nuanced decision and it's not one of the other for everyone. For a lot of people I would say just keep it on the same page.
